He cautioned that the development could set a dangerous precedent for opposition politics, insisting that every political party and candidate had a stake in protecting democratic participation and the people’s right to choose their leaders.
The AA presidential candidate, in a statement on Friday, November 6, 2026, described the Federal High Court judgment nullifying the leadership of the African Democratic Congress (ADC) under former Senate President David Mark and invalidating the presidential nomination of former Vice President Atiku Abubakar as troubling.
He said the timing of the judgment, barely two and a half months before the 2027 general elections, had raised serious questions about judicial independence, political competition and the future of Nigeria’s democracy.
Fadojoe stressed that his reaction was not based on party affiliation, noting that he was not a member of the ADC but believed that an injustice against democratic participation in one party could threaten the rights of other opposition candidates.
On the role of the judiciary, Fadojoe acknowledged the importance of the courts in upholding the Constitution and ensuring that political actors operate within the law.
“Why has Nigeria become a country where political parties spend more time defending their existence in courtrooms than presenting solutions to the Nigerian people?” he queried.
He also questioned why elections were increasingly becoming entangled in prolonged litigation, factional disputes and last-minute judicial pronouncements.
The AA presidential candidate maintained that no political party or candidate should be above the law, but insisted that judicial decisions must take into account their broader implications for democratic participation.
Fadojoe consequently called for urgent measures to restore public confidence in the independence, consistency and impartiality of the Nigerian judicial system.
He urged President Tinubu and the APC to recognise that Nigerians were closely monitoring developments within the country’s political landscape.
He maintained that the survival of Nigeria’s democracy depended on protecting political plurality, strengthening democratic institutions and ensuring that voters, rather than institutional controversies, ultimately determined the country’s political leadership.
